## Optical measurement set-up

A spatial filtering set-up (Thorlabs, AC127-019-A; Thorlabs, P10CB) was used to generate a clean Gaussian beam from the incident laser. The collimated beam was then passed through a linear polarizer (Thorlabs, LPVISE050-A) followed by a quarter-wave plate (Thorlabs, AQWP05M-600) to produce LCP light. The LCP beam was normally incident on the metalens, and the transmitted light was collected by a commercial objective lens (Olympus, 1-U2M350). An analyser was inserted between the objective and the tube lens to isolate the conjugate RCP component corresponding to the point spread function (Thorlabs, TTL180-A). ## Discussion

In summary, we demonstrate metalens fabrication at an industrial scale using a custom-built R2R nanoimprinter in a cost-effective, fully automated and high-throughput manner, with a throughput as high as 300 lenses per second (Supplementary Table 1). By carefully optimizing the mould preparation and key process parameters—including web speed, tension and imprinting conditions—we have successfully implemented an R2R system for metalens production, achieving feature resolution down to 80 nm. By applying a hybrid material composed of UV-curable resin and a conformal TiO $_{2}$ thin film, the optical performance of the metalenses has been significantly improved, achieving about 49% efficiency across a full 300-mm wafer.

## Pilot line for R2R manufacturing of visible metalenses

The complete R2R process of metalenses starts by dispensing and uniformly coating UV resin on the running PET film, followed by an imprinting process in which the film is pressed against the imprinting roller, with the pressure controlled by the counter roller and irradiated with UV light to cure the resin. results.heading: Design principle of metalens
results.snippet:
## Design principle of metalens

A 0–2π phase modulation of the metalens is achieved by rotating anisotropic meta-atoms by an angle of θ, which is known as the Pancharatnam–Berry phase. An anisotropic meta-atom rotated by an angle θ can be theoretically modeled using a Jones matrix. When right circularly polarized (RCP) light is incident, the complex transmittance can be expressed as follows (Supplementary Note 2).

$$
E _ {\mathrm{T}} = \frac {t _ {x x} + t _ {y y}}{2} \left[ \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ - i \end{array} \right] + \frac {t _ {x x} - t _ {y y}}{2} e ^ {- i 2 \theta} \left[ \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ i \end{array} \right]\tag{1}
$$

results.heading: Manufacturing workflow
results.snippet:
## Manufacturing workflow

A schematic of the manufacturing workflow is shown in Fig. 1a. In step 1, a 300-mm wafer master stamp comprising 450 dies of 1-cm-diameter metalenses is fabricated using an ArF immersion scanner with a 4× reticle (Fig. 1ai, left). Next, a flexible replica mould is directly fabricated by UV-NIL using a master stamp (Fig. 1ai, right, and Extended Data Fig. 1). In step 2, the flexible replica mould is applied to our custom-built R2R-UV-NIL system, which is composed of three sections: resin coating, imprinting-curing unit and rewinding (Fig. 1aii and Supplementary Note 1). results.heading: Master template preparation
results.snippet:
## Master template preparation

The initial template comprised molybdenum silicide deposited on a silica substrate. Metalens patterns were created using a high-resolution electron-beam lithography system (JBX Series, JEOL) to expose the positive photoresist (FEP series, Fujifilm). Following exposure, patterns were developed using a tetramethylammonium solution. Molybdenum silicide was then deposited to a thickness of 69 nm via electron beam evaporation, using a silicon substrate as the cluster formation template. Pattern transfer was accomplished using ArF immersion lithography (XT-1900Gi, ASML) on positive photoresists, followed by development in a tetramethylammonium solution.
